q.young: Did something get splashed in your eye?
q.older: Did something get splashed into your eye?

candidates.why: Item 1, plain form: decision 1 rules 'splashed' as the register word, and this asks the event with no substance named at all, which is the default the item-1 exception sits on top of.

q.young: Did something from a bottle go in your eye?
q.older: Did something from a bottle or spray get into your eye?

candidates.why: Item 1 using decision 3's narrow category cue ('something from a bottle', 'a spray') because 'chemical' is not a word a 4-year-old owns and RCH injury puts irrigation before examination; no substance is named.

q.young: Did something go into your eye?
q.older: Did something go into your eye, even something small?

candidates.why: Item 2 as a mechanism question in decision 1's words ('got into your eye'); 'even something small' carries source 3's retained intraocular fragment without naming an object, since the item-1 exception is not extended here.

q.young: Did anything fly into your eye?
q.older: Did anything fly or shoot into your eye?

candidates.why: Item 2 aimed at the high-velocity half of source 2's projectile list and source 6's Box 1 'High-velocity injury', carried by the verb rather than by naming any of the banned objects.

q.young: Did something hit or bump your eye?
q.older: Did something hit your eye or bump into it?

candidates.why: Item 3, the blunt mechanism source 3 keeps apart from projectile ('blunt force/sharp object/projectile') and source 6 calls 'a physical impact'; phrased about the object, never about a person, per the safeguarding exclusion.

q.young: Did you bump your eye on something?
q.older: Did you fall or bump your eye on something hard?

candidates.why: Item 3 reached from the child's own movement, which is how an unwitnessed injury at home reaches the nurse (source 2: 'Most injuries occur at home away from parental supervision'); non-attributive, no second person in the sentence.

q.young: Is anything blurry or hard to see?
q.older: Is anything looking blurry or hard to see right now?

candidates.why: Item 4 in the shipped `blurry` wording so decision 11's re-sourcing carries it across with citations; no eye-covering or comparison, so it stays a report and not the measured acuity of item 23.

q.young: Do things look funny or fuzzy now?
q.older: Do things look fuzzy or different from before?

candidates.why: Item 4 in NHS source 12's family-facing register ('changes in your vision') for a child who does not own the word blurry; says nothing about losing sight, which the cautions ban outright.

q.older: Does bright light make your eyes hurt?

candidates.why: Item 5 in decision 1's words ('light hurts your eyes', 'bright light'), and tagged with the `light-hurts` fact decision 10 requires so the head group's hand-written question dedupes against it.

q.young: Does it feel like something is in your eye?
q.older: Does it feel like something is in your eye, like sand?

candidates.why: Item 6 in the exact concept source 11 cognitive-tested and found 'clear and easy to understand', with decision 1's older-tier 'like sand' in place of the banned 'gritty'.

q.older: Does your eye feel scratchy, like sand got in it?

candidates.why: Item 6 for a child who would not build the longer sentence; keeps the sensation separate from item 2's event, which is the split source 1's '(corneal process)' parenthesis earns.

q.young: Is it hard to keep your eye open?
q.older: Is it hard to keep your eye open right now?

candidates.why: Item 7 as the child's half of source 5's 'the child will often be reluctant to open their eye' — a thing the child notices about themselves, with no instruction to open, hold open or test the eye.

q.young: Was your eye stuck shut when you woke up?
q.older: Was your eye stuck shut or stuck together when you woke up?

candidates.why: Item 8, source 7's 'glued eyes in the morning' in decision 1's register ('stuck shut' / 'stuck together', never 'glued' or 'sticky eye'); the morning framing carries the fact without naming what is on the lashes.

q.young: Were your eyelashes stuck shut this morning?
q.older: Were your eyelashes stuck together when you woke up today?

candidates.why: Item 8 from NHS source 12's family-facing 'pus that sticks to lashes', reworded to the visible lashes so no substance is named; five-band duration because source 7 excludes symptoms over seven days.

candidates.why: Item 10 with the ordinary act in the subject position, so nothing in the sentence can be read as an instruction to move the eyes; the packet's worst-sourced item, flagged for the reviewer either way.
